title: New Bigfoot documentary brings Yakima connections into focus
excerpt: For a city surrounded by shrub steppe, Yakima has an outsized connection to the forest-dwelling Sasquatch.
content:
For a city surrounded by shrub steppe, Yakima has an outsized connection to the forest-dwelling Sasquatch.

The link comes from the grainy 1967 Patterson-Gimlin film, which purports to be the first footage of Bigfoot in the wild. As the story goes, two Yakima Valley residents claimed they found and filmed the creature in Northern California. Another local resident decades later claimed that it was a hoax and it was him in a gorilla suit the whole time. 

Now, nearly 60 years later, a new documentary is diving deep into those stories, interviewing some of the people associated with the Patterson-Gimlin film, as well as unearthing newly discovered footage that could change the narrative about how the footage came to be.

“Capturing Bigfoot” will be available for streaming on Amazon Video starting Oct. 20. A special screening with the director and subjects of the film is planned at 7 p.m. on Oct. 24 at The Majestic Theatre in Union Gap.

The movie premiered at the South by Southwest festival in Texas in March. 

Bigfoot on camera

Marq Evans, who directed "Capturing Bigfoot," teaches documentary filmmaking at Olympic College in Bremerton and has made documentaries about baseball cards and Claymation in the past.

“The idea for this film kind of fell into my lap,” he said in an interview with the Herald-Republic. 

Roger Patterson of Yakima was “a chronically unemployed ex-rodeo cowboy” and a Bigfoot enthusiast who self-published a book on the subject, "Do abominable snowmen of America really exist?" in 1966.

“When Roger Patterson was active in the Bigfoot field in Yakima, Bigfoot seemed to be in Yakima quite a bit,” Evans said. “Make of that what you will.”

On Oct. 20, 1967, Patterson and Bob Gimlin, also of the Yakima area, were on horseback in the woods near Butte Creek in Northern California looking for Bigfoot, as there had been claims of large footprints in the area.

They said they suddenly came across the beast striding across a creek bed and captured it on film. They also made plaster casts of its tracks.

With the minute-long footage, they went to Los Angeles 12 days later and formed Bigfoot Enterprises, a company which sold the licensing rights to the film.

Albert E. DeAtley Jr., a prominent Yakima paving contractor, loaned Patterson (his brother-in-law) money to make the film. DeAtley had an ownership stake in Patterson's film company for a few years before withdrawing from it. He later said that he never asked if the film was real or not. 

Patterson died in 1972 of cancer. Gimlin, a Korean War veteran and horse trainer, has on many occasions denied that the footage was a hoax while also expressing regret for being associated with it. 

Things soured between the friends. In 1975, Gimlin sued DeAtley and Patterson's widow, Patricia, claiming he wasn't receiving his share of the film's proceeds. The lawsuit was settled out of court, the Yakima Herald-Republic reported in 1999.  

Though the Patterson-Gimlin film forever shaped the public’s conception of Bigfoot, folklore about ape men has long been documented around the world. “Sasquatch” is a term that comes from the Sts'ailes people in British Columbia. Ape Canyon, near Mount St. Helens, is said to have been named for a violent encounter between apelike men and gold prospectors in 1924.

Many loggers in the 20th century claimed to have come across large human-like footprints in the woods, adding to the legend. 

In 2004, Yakima resident Bob Heironimus told the press that the Patterson-Gimlin film was a hoax and that he wore a gorilla suit at the behest of the duo. He told his story in a book “The Making of Bigfoot.” Heironimus told the Yakima Herald-Republic that he promised Patterson he would keep his role a secret, though he said he was never paid the $1,000 he said he was promised.

In 2012, both Gimlin and Heironimus were interviewed by the Yakima Herald-Republic, and both stuck to their versions of the story.

Their stories will featured in “Capturing Bigfoot.” It has interviews with Roger Patterson’s son, Clint Patterson; Patterson’s widow, Patricia; Gimlin and Heironimus.

Stumbling upon new footage

Evans, along with his wife and son, make up The McCaw Studio, a family partnership through which they have produced both films and books.

Evans took on the subject of the Patterson-Gimlin film for a few reasons. For one, his parents were Yakima residents and he spent the first few years of his life here. Evans said that he had heard tales about the Bigfoot film from his father, who once worked for DeAtley's paving company.

But the story Evans heard around the campfire from his father growing up took on new urgency when a colleague asked him in 2022 to process old film her late father kept in his safe.

“She thought it was from the '60s, and that it was related to or was the famous Patterson-Gimlin film, and that was based off stories that she heard from her dad as a kid,” Evans said. But after processing and viewing it, he realized it was different.

“This is not the famous film we all know. We found out it's dated from 1966, and it's got a heck of a lot of similarities. So then the question was, well, what is it? And that's really what kicked this whole thing off,” Evans said.

But what really made the story a compelling subject was the interesting cast of characters from Yakima, Evans said.

“This new film and the mystery behind that is obviously what pulled me in, but I don’t know if it necessarily would have turned into a film and three-plus years of my time if it weren’t for those 'characters' of Roger Patterson and Bob Gimlin and some of these other people; Roger’s cowboy buddies from the place I was born,” Evans said.

Evans cites the book “The Making of Bigfoot” as an inspiration for how he approached the story.

“The book I thought did a good job of creating these characters that I could visualize in a movie,” Evans said. Greg Long, the book’s author, appears in the documentary.

Disproving Bigfoot was not a part of the agenda, Evans said, though the film has generated plenty of discussion among Bigfoot believers.

“It was just this really fascinating story about the people involved in creating the most famous Bigfoot film of all time. What was the real story behind that? And then trying to figure out this new piece of footage. How does it connect? If it does connect, what does that say? That’s what got the Bigfoot community all riled up,” Evans said.

But his story is less about Bigfoot, and more about people.

“For me, it’s a story about friendship and betrayal and reunions and family; promises kept and broken promises; all of those human nature things that I think make it a strong film and what excites me about the film more than anything else,” Evans said.

Questen Inghram is a reporter at the Yakima Herald-Republic whose beat focuses on water, the environment, and Lower Valley communities. Email qinghram@yakimaherald.com or call 509-577-7674.
